rule: mixed: the rule fires, but 'in winter' ends up on the derived slowing instead of in the condition, so nothing gates the claim on the season, and the bare definite 'the burn' becomes one particular burning that every salt-bloom is then said to slow. Say what burns and put winter into a condition clause: 'When salt-bloom is added to mire-essence in winter, the mire-essence burns slowly.'
texts: bad: 'the Keepers' becomes an anonymous group of keepers - the name is dropped and a member kind is invented - and the rule's condition then requires a member of that private group, which no other sentence can ever supply, so the rule is dead in practice; the slow burning is also left unlinked to the addition that triggers it. Use a singular actor so the condition ranges over keepers in general: 'When a Keeper adds salt-bloom to mire-essence in winter, that mire-essence burns slowly.'

good. the condition is a plain matchable mixing event, 'the Keepers' keeps its name as one stable symbol (so later sentences about them join up), and the slow burning is tied back to the mixing occasion, with the 'into' goal, the season and the manner adverb all carried.

bad: with an ordinary verb, 'a salt-bloomed lantern' reads as one particular lantern, so the parse records a single episode - this lantern resisted this wind - and the general world rule is lost. Use a bare plural, which is what makes it a generic: 'Salt-bloomed lanterns resist cold winds.'
